fields.title: Competitors: how they grow, not what features they have
fields.keyTakeaway: Feature matrix comparisons explain almost nothing. What explains success is the growth mechanism: where their clients come from, why they stay, and what lets them defend pricing. And you need to analyze more than just lookalike products.
fields.checkQuestion: A competitor has twice as many features at half the price. What question should you ask first?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how do competitors scale?**
fields.blocks/1/subtitle: Who is actually eroding your margins
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **Industry rivalry** — number of similar players and how they compete: on price or something else.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **New entrants** — barrier to entry. If low, high margins do not last long.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: **Substitutes** — alternative ways to solve the problem. For Kedr, that is Excel and hiring a manual inventory clerk — and they are far more dangerous than direct rivals.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: **Supplier power** — who you depend on: cloud provider, payment gateway, data provider.
fields.blocks/1/items/4: **Buyer power** — whether clients can push down prices. Depends on client size and switching costs.
fields.blocks/2/text: A **Competition Map** visualizes this positioning along two axes that matter to clients. Use axes reflecting real customer buying criteria, not convenient comparisons.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Competitor Yarus has been outgrowing us for three years. Team's initial take: "they have more features."

Deep dive revealed:
— 60% of their leads come from eight systems integrator partners who get 20% of first-year revenue. We have no partner channel.
— Their subscription price is lower because implementation is unbundled at 300 thousand; total year-one client spend is actually higher than ours.
— Churn is low: three years of data and trained staff create high switching costs.

Their growth engine is distribution, not features. Copying features is useless; the real question is whether to build our own partner channel.
fields.blocks/4/text: Half of Kedr's lost deals are lost not to Yarus, but to "let us stick with Excel for now." The substitute is free, familiar, and bypasses budget approvals — that is the true alternative to compete against.
fields.blocks/4/title: The primary competitor is not software
fields.blocks/5/text: Competitor analysis explains current and past market dynamics. It does not predict future moves or replace a position of your own: a strategy of "copying the leader, but slightly better" loses by default.
